item.research_question: How can the deformation mechanisms (TRIP vs. TWIP) in face-centered cubic high-entropy alloys be accurately predicted to overcome the strength-ductility trade-off, given the limitations of the intrinsic stacking fault energy (ISFE) criterion?
item.material_system: Co-Cr-Fe-Mn-Ni high-entropy alloys (specifically CoxCr44-xFe26Mn10Ni8 and Co36CrxFe46-xMn10Ni8 series) and literature-reported TRIP/TWIP steels
item.processing_route: Arc melting of high-purity elements followed by homogenization at 1200°C for 1 hour and water quenching; cold rolling with 60% thickness reduction; uniaxial compression at 20% strain with a strain rate of 10⁻³ s⁻¹
item.test_conditions: Room temperature (293 K) for thermodynamic calculations; microstructure characterized via EBSD and HRTEM after deformation; hardness measured using Vickers microhardness tester (100 gram-force, 10-s dwelling time)
key_findings: The traditional ISFE criterion fails to predict deformation mechanisms in more than 50% of the studied cases, with an accuracy of only about 56%.
The proposed UMFE/UTFE criterion accurately predicts the deformation mechanisms (TRIP vs. TWIP) in all 7 designed HEAs and tested steels, achieving 100% accuracy.
Seven new HEAs were successfully designed and experimentally verified to exhibit either TRIP or TWIP behavior based on the UMFE < UTFE or UMFE > UTFE criteria.
Co content increases the energy barrier for stacking fault and twin formation (USFE and UTFE) but decreases ISFE, UMFE, and ME energy.
Ni content exhibits a strong effect on increasing ISFE, ESFE/TEE, UMFE, and MEE, limiting its content to promote the TRIP effect.
TRIP-dominant alloys show higher hardness compared to TWIP-dominant alloys, with hardness increasing after deformation due to high-strain hardening.

In TWIP steels, the calculated ISFE was -289.2 mJ/m², making it impossible to predict the mechanism, whereas UTFE (107.3 mJ/m²) was much smaller than UMFE (243.6 mJ/m²), correctly indicating twinning dominance.
item.mechanism: The competition between martensitic transformation and twinning is governed by the energy barriers defined by the difference between unstable fault energies and ISFE (UMFE-ISFE and UTFE-ISFE). Martensitic transformation prevails when the unstable martensite fault energy (UMFE) is smaller than the unstable twin fault energy (UTFE), while deformation twinning dominates if UMFE is larger than UTFE. These unstable fault energies represent the energy barriers for the formation of martensite and twin embryos, respectively, which ISFE does not capture.
item.limitations: The study did not test tensile properties, which are more appropriate to evaluate the mechanical properties of the designed HEAs. Discrepancies between CALPHAD-based thermodynamic models and DFT calculations regarding fcc stability exist and could be reduced by more advanced models considering interfacial energy.
item.future_work: To perform systematic mechanical property evaluation, specifically tensile testing, to select the best HEAs with potential applications and to accelerate the discovery of TRIP/TWIP in a wide spectrum of alloys using the proposed design paradigm.
quotes: Among the studied HEAs and steels, the traditional ISFE criterion fails in more than half of the cases, while the UMFE/UTFE criterion accurately predicts the deformation mechanisms in all cases.
The energy difference between UMFE and ISFE is the energy barrier for ME formation.
The condition UMFE < UTFE has a strong positive correlation with TRIP and a strong negative correlation with TWIP.
